# Deepfake Summary
Deepfake technology originates from earlier advancements in photo manipulation and motion pictures, steadily improving with digital video. The technology has evolved from academic research in the 1990s into tools used by amateurs online and subsequently adopted by industry. Deepfakes are created using neural networks, particularly autoencoders, which feature an encoder to reduce an image to a latent space and a decoder to reconstruct it. A common advancement involves attaching a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to the decoder, which forces the generator to produce highly realistic images.
The proliferation of deepfakes raises significant concerns across various domains. Socially and ethically, they are viewed as an "epistemic threat" to knowledge, capable of undermining trust in information and interfering with democratic functions. Malicious uses include blackmail, fraud (with scams estimated to reach $40 Billion in the next three years), and political misinformation campaigns designed to influence voters. While detection methods—such as identifying software-induced artifacts in videos or using deep learning on audio—are advancing, experts note the continuous evolution of deepfake generation makes detection a "moving goal post." Potential countermeasures include media literacy education and regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which mandates transparency for AI-generated content.
